soil-agri-086.title: SSURGO, the database behind US soil surveys
soil-agri-086.text: The soil surveys that once filled county books now sit in a database. SSURGO, the Soil Survey Geographic database, is digital soil data produced and distributed by the NRCS. It is the dataset in which the NRCS maintains its soil information. It records soil types and where they occur, their characteristics and properties, and their limits, risks and suitability for various uses. Its data reach users through the online service described in {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, which the NRCS runs as the single authoritative source of US soil survey information.

soil-agri-107.title: The ard, an ox-drawn scratch plough
soil-agri-107.text: Oxen domesticated in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BC, supplied the draft power that made the ard possible. The ard is the early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share, a cutting blade, through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow. A ploughed field from about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan, India. The ard left undisturbed strips between furrows, so fields were cross-ploughed both ways, which tended to form the squarish plots described in {{ref:soil-hist-099}}. It suits loamy or sandy soils renewed by floods, as in the Nile Delta and Fertile Crescent, and it struggled in northern Europe's heavy soils.

soil-bio-009.title: What acid, salt and the plow do to soil life
soil-bio-009.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike. Threats to soil biodiversity are soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinization, sodicity, structure decline and erosion. Many are driven by how soil is managed. Acidification cuts the numbers of most large soil animals, earthworms included. It harms the survival of the bacteria covered in {{ref:soil-bio-239}} and may slow decay and the capture of nitrogen from the air. Salt works differently. At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less. Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and breaking down soil organic matter more slowly. Erosion strips topsoil, soil organic matter and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat. Constant {{ref:soil-agri-095}} redistributes soil organic matter, degrading structure and altering populations of earthworms and other organisms. Even a common fertilizer can harm. Chloride from potassium chloride raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, including the bacteria that make nitrate.

soil-bio-018.title: Farming with microbes: promise and pitfalls
soil-bio-018.text: Healthy soil life can supply crops with nutrients such as nitrogen and protect them against pests and diseases, while reducing the need for water and other inputs. Using and managing soil microorganisms toward those ends is the agricultural use of soil microbes. The partnership is fragile. Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots. Excess fertilizer, phosphorus above a threshold in particular, can suppress the fungi that partner with roots and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors. Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market. Long-marketed examples include Trichoderma fungi, which suppress disease-causing fungi, and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis. The field is hard going. Many strains that look promising in the lab fail outdoors because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects. Introduced populations can fade, as Bacillus subtilis does when it lacks a niche it can defend. Using several collaborating strains helps. Rules demanding safety evidence have even led many products to call themselves by the label discussed in {{ref:soil-fert-205}} rather than 'biopesticides'.

soil-bio-047.title: Bioturbation: how burrowers stir the earth
soil-bio-047.text: In the 1800s Darwin watched a field slowly swallow a layer of chalk. Spread on the surface, the chalk lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year that he credited to earthworms. That began the formal study of bioturbation: the reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains. Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaete worms, shrimps and midge larvae dominate. Bioturbation differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and dissolved substances in sediments, which is one of its effects. Burrowers carry oxygen into oxygen-poor layers, changing how microbes live and speeding the breakdown of soil organic matter. Their burrows shelter other species. The process profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity. Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees to the story in 1891. Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil science and the study of landforms since the 1980s. The process itself is far older. Since it began around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion. Pollution can run it backward. When pollution harms earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the {{ref:soil-bio-095}} shifts toward mor.

soil-bio-064.title: Three degrees of control in living mineral-making
soil-bio-064.text: Living things build minerals with very different degrees of control. One scheme, following a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues, sorts {{ref:soil-bio-063}} into three kinds. In the biologically controlled kind, the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location. Mollusc and brachiopod shells are built this way. In the biologically induced kind, the metabolic activity of microbes, covered in {{ref:soil-bio-208}}, creates chemical conditions that favor mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete. Stromatolites and other microbial mats form like this. In the biologically influenced kind, abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals. The terms have no standardized definitions, and their use varies widely.

soil-bio-077.title: Sorting bacteria by how they eat and breathe
soil-bio-077.text: Bacteria can be sorted by three questions: where their energy comes from, which electron donors they use and where they get their carbon. Electrons are the currency of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Phototrophs get their energy from light by photosynthesis, while the organisms of {{ref:soil-bio-205}} get it by oxidizing chemical compounds. Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are covered in {{ref:soil-bio-056}}; those that use organic compounds are the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-206}}. Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide. Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide. Facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

soil-bio-115.title: Decomposition, the breakdown that recycles the living world
soil-bio-115.text: Rotting plants release over 90 percent of the carbon dioxide given off each year. That rotting is decomposition: the breakdown of dead organic substances into simpler matter such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts. It recycles the finite matter of the biosphere. Chemical or physical forces drive abiotic decomposition. Living organisms, mostly microbes, drive biotic decomposition, the process traced in {{ref:soil-env-231}}. Plant matter decays in stages. Water first leaches out the soluble carbon compounds. Soil invertebrates then fragment the litter, and microbes chemically alter what remains. In soil the reactions fall into three groups. Enzymes oxidize compounds to carbon dioxide, water and heat; nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are released; and resistant compounds form that make up {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. The rate depends on temperature, moisture, soil properties, the amount and quality of dead material, and the microbes themselves. Decay is slow in very wet or very dry soil and fastest in damp soil with enough oxygen. When dry soil is rewetted, many bacterial cells burst and release a pulse of nutrients. Materials differ too. Sugars and amino acids are labile, quick to break down. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-232}} are moderately labile. In a temperate climate their half-life is 12–18 days. {{ref:soil-bio-116}} and {{ref:soil-bio-233}} resist, so resistant material builds up as soil organic matter ages. Acid and clay-rich soils decompose organic matter more slowly, because clay binds it out of microbes' reach. Turning the soil speeds decay by adding oxygen and exposing fresh organic matter.

soil-bio-141.title: Root mucilage, the slime that greases every root tip
soil-bio-141.text: Plants use up to 40% of the energy they make by photosynthesis secreting one product: slime. Root mucilage is a gelatinous secretion of plant-specific polysaccharides, long chains of sugars, that coats the protective tip described in {{ref:soil-bio-198}} as part of the root exudate. How it is secreted is still debated. Growing evidence points to root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing polysaccharides made in their Golgi apparatus and cell walls. Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose, the building blocks of pectin and other plant polysaccharides. Mucilage glues soil to the root, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake. It cuts friction as roots penetrate and maintains a microclimate. It can also reduce evaporation and store water, which helps plants cope with water deficit. Soil fungi feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.

soil-bio-159.title: Inside the cell or around it: the kinds of mycorrhiza
soil-bio-159.text: The first question about any mycorrhiza is how far the fungus gets into the root. Mycorrhizal types group these partnerships by how the fungus colonizes the root. The main split runs between {{ref:soil-bio-173}} and endomycorrhizas. In the first kind, the hyphae never enter individual root cells. In endomycorrhizas they pass through the cell wall, up to the cell membrane. The endomycorrhizas include the types described in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}, {{ref:soil-bio-176}} and {{ref:soil-bio-186}}, along with arbutoid and monotropoid forms. The lifestyle evolved independently many times. The fungi of the first of those endomycorrhizal types form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life. Not every fungus inside a root is a partner of this kind. Fungal {{ref:soil-bio-202}} live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside. Mucoromycotina fungi of this kind, living in the roots described in {{ref:soil-bio-242}}, were long mistaken for partners of the first type. They seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils. In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the flow runs backward. The plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

soil-bio-193.title: Nematodes, the most numerous animals on Earth
soil-bio-193.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion for every person. Nematodes are roundworms, or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda. Most live freely and feed on microbes, but many are parasites. They often exceed a million individuals per square meter, and they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth. Densities peak in tundra and boreal forests. About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm. They do not break down dead material. They eat living things instead, up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, and so regulate bacterial numbers and the mix of bacterial kinds. By releasing nitrogen in mineral form, they can play an important part in the movement of nitrogen through soil. They are prey too: the fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-215}} trap them with lassos or sticky structures, or release toxins on contact. Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million. The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism. In 2023 a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

soil-chem-082.title: Telling one clay from another in the laboratory
soil-chem-082.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study. X-ray diffraction is the main tool for identifying them, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. To put numbers on a soil's clays, analysts first measure its soil organic matter, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals. They then estimate clay percentages from how much glycol a sample takes up, {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, K2O and thermal data. This glycol test, a case of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites over eight hours of exposure to the vapor at 60 °C. Illite is estimated from its potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.

soil-chem-104.title: Goethite, the iron mineral in rust and yellow soils
soil-chem-104.text: Every patch of rust holds a soil mineral. Goethite is the α form of the iron(III) oxide-hydroxide FeO(OH). It is the main component of rust and of bog iron ore, which forms in swampy ground at the head of springs. In soil it often forms by weathering of other iron-rich minerals. As iron-bearing minerals reach the soil's oxidation zone, ferrous iron(II) becomes ferric iron(III). The parent mineral's shape is kept, so goethite often forms pseudomorphs, crystals in another mineral's outline. Some bacteria make it too. It is concentrated in {{ref:soil-form-065}}, alongside quartz and other iron and clay minerals. Goethite is yellowish to reddish to dark brown or black, and it helps tint soils yellow to red. Its grip on nutrients is fierce: clays rich in goethite hold phosphorus so tightly that plants cannot absorb it. Heating converts it to {{ref:soil-chem-166}}, which raises soil magnetism. Long used as the pigment brown ochre, it was first described in 1806 and named after Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

soil-chem-113.title: Redox: the electron trade behind rust and breath
soil-chem-113.text: A rusting nail and a breathing animal run the same kind of chemistry. Redox, short for reduction–oxidation, is any reaction in which the reactants' electron bookkeeping, set out in {{ref:soil-chem-178}}, changes. Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in that bookkeeping number. Reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in it. The two always happen together. Neither can occur on its own. When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide, while oxygen is reduced by taking up the electrons the iron releases. The same trade powers respiration, photosynthesis, combustion and the corrosion of metals. The words are older than the idea of the electron. Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen. Reduction meant the weight lost when ore is heated to extract its metal. Both were later widened to mean electron transfer. The word redox itself first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. In soils, sediments and water, redox differs from place to place. Those differences drive the cycling of elements through living things and their surroundings, as {{ref:soil-chem-121}} shows.

soil-chem-120.title: Rust spots and gray streaks: redox written in soil color
soil-chem-120.text: A soil's colors can record years of wetting and drying. Redoximorphic features are color patterns made when iron or manganese is oxidized, reduced and moved, so pigment is lost or gained against the soil's background color, its matrix. A matrix colored by ferrous iron, the reduced form, also counts. A pattern earns the name only once the processes behind it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions leave disrupted color: complex mottles and points of concentrated color. Aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes instead. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. These features extend the story of {{ref:soil-found-028}} and give critical information for interpreting soils. The voltage measured in a soil, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-123}}, expresses how likely such reactions are. Classification relies on them too. Among the cracking clay soils of {{ref:soil-class-106}}, those with {{ref:soil-class-155}} and these features form one named group, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them.

soil-class-002.title: How engineers classify soil to build on it
soil-class-002.text: To an engineer, soil is a material to build on or to build with. Engineering soil classification groups soils by the properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material. Modern systems are designed to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave. In North America the most common is the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS. It and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487. Europe's standard, {{ref:soil-class-152}}, closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently. It also adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays. In the United States, the {{ref:soil-class-036}} rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction. The Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties. Moderately organic soils count as subdivisions of silts and clays. They are told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying. A full geotechnical description goes further than any code. It adds color, moisture and strength in place, and more detail about the material than the USCS code carries.

soil-class-145.title: Technosols, the soils of cities, mines and dumps
soil-class-145.text: A landfill, a heap of mine spoil and a city pavement can all count as soil. Technosols are soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin. A Technosol holds a significant amount of artifacts, objects made by people, or has a geotechnical liner, or is sealed by technic hard material unlike natural rock. The group covers soils of landfills, sludge, cinders, mine spoil and ash, pavements with their underlying material, and the engineered soils covered in {{ref:soil-class-157}}. Natural soil that has merely been transported does not count. Often called urban or mine soils, Technosols occur near cities, roads, mines, dumps, oil spills and fly-ash deposits, usually in small patches. They can change fast: a Technosol can differentiate A and O horizons at more than one centimeter per year. They are more likely than other soils to be contaminated, and many must be handled with care because of toxic industrial substances. Some are made on purpose to cover wastes such as mine tailings, as at Andacollo in Chile. Their closest relatives are {{ref:soil-class-120}}, soils created by long-term measures to raise fertility for farming.

soil-env-024.title: Bioventing: helping soil microbes breathe
soil-env-024.text: Microbes readily break down gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuel when oxygen is plentiful. Bioventing supplies that oxygen, raising the flow of air into the unsaturated zone to speed the natural in situ breakdown of hydrocarbons. It is the commonest aerobic bioremediation. Oxygen serves as the electron acceptor that oxidizes petroleum, PAHs, phenols and other reduced pollutants. Heavier molecules are harder for microbes to break down, a process covered in {{ref:soil-env-231}}. The method is inexpensive, but cleaning a site can take a few years. Below the water table oxygen is scarcer, because water in equilibrium with air holds only 8 to 10 mg/L. There it comes from aerated water, pure oxygen, peroxides or bubbled air, the method of {{ref:soil-env-240}}.

soil-env-054.title: In situ thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of the ground
soil-env-054.text: Soil heated in place to as much as 900 °C gives up its pollutants by vaporization, steam distillation, oxidation or pyrolysis. This in-place form of {{ref:soil-env-230}}, also called thermal conduction heating, does exactly that, sometimes under vacuum. Arrays of electric or gas-fired thermal wells heat the soil by conduction, and vapor extraction wells collect the released contaminants. It works in tight soils such as clay, above and below the water table, at temperatures from under 100 °C to above the boiling point of water. Shell Oil developed it in the late 1980s from research on enhanced oil recovery, and commercialized it in the mid-1990s.

soil-env-216.title: The septic tank: sewage treatment in a buried chamber
soil-env-216.text: In 2008 about 20 percent of US households relied on a septic tank. It is an underground chamber of concrete, fiberglass or plastic where household sewage gets primary treatment. Solids settle and are digested without oxygen in the first chamber. The liquid flows to a septic drain field, whose soil must pass a percolation test. Sludge outpaces decomposition, so a vacuum truck removes it every few years, or every 10-20 years in some systems. Tanks remove little nitrogen. Soils usually retain phosphorus, but sandy soils near water can saturate and pass it on, risking {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Dense development can push the contamination traced in {{ref:soil-env-242}} past acceptable limits.

soil-fert-014.title: The hidden bill for feeding the world's crops
soil-fert-014.text: Fertilizer washing off farmland helps create dead zones in the ocean. That is one of the direct costs of fertilizers, whose production and use harm water, soil, air and ecosystems. It also contaminates waterways, the soil microbiome degrades and toxic compounds accumulate. Indirect costs reach further: nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for the gas the Haber process needs, and the biodiversity and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture. The climate pays too. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying the hydrogen for ammonia. The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and its associated land use among the drivers of global warming. Organic sources are not blameless, since too much pig slurry can contaminate aquifers and overfeed the waters they supply. Solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives for production. On the farm, plowing less and planting the streamside borders of {{ref:soil-agri-158}} can lessen the damage. Policy favors sustainable or regenerative farming, with less synthetic fertilizer, better care of the soil and more of the biological fertilizers in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}.

soil-fert-083.title: The salt index: how hard a fertilizer pulls on water
soil-fert-083.text: Potassium chloride has a salt index of 116.2. Urea scores 74.4, and the fertilizer in {{ref:soil-fert-206}} scores 29.2. The fertilizer salt index measures how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, the pull dissolved salts exert, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100. Fertilizers with an index above 20 are not recommended for particularly sensitive crops. Using too much fertilizer, or one with too high an index, builds up salts in the soil and causes burns.

soil-fert-126.title: The nitrogen cascade: one atom, many harms
soil-fert-126.text: The same nitrogen can cause trouble again and again. The nitrogen cascade is the passage of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next, with effects at each step. Most reactive nitrogen applied to farmland cascades through air, water and land until {{ref:soil-fert-108}} turns it back into nitrogen gas. That final microbial step matters, because the atmosphere is the ultimate sink for reactive nitrogen. Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying its local effects. Managed vegetated borders, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-158}}, and wet areas can remove much of the nitrate leaving farms, damping the cascade.

soil-fert-166.title: Plant tissue analysis: asking the crop instead of the soil
soil-fert-166.text: Sometimes the surest way to learn what a soil supplies is to analyze the plant. Plant tissue analysis describes a plant's nutrient status, also called its ionome or nutrient profile. Interpreting the results has been controversial. In recent decades, mathematical models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced the nearly two-century-old Liebig's law in this work. Tissue tests can identify nitrogen deficiencies, and sensing chlorophyll content allows variable nitrogen rates during the season. Analysis can also reveal a shortage of boron, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-226}}, early enough to correct it. Once symptoms appear, crop loss cannot be prevented.

soil-form-010.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone
soil-form-010.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, because it holds less soil organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and soil-forming processes have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.

soil-form-025.title: Hardpans, the buried floors that stop roots
soil-form-025.text: Some soils have a floor that roots and water cannot get through. A hardpan is a dense, largely water-impervious layer, usually lying just below the topsoil. Some form naturally, when deposits such as dissolved silica, {{ref:soil-chem-163}} or calcium carbonate fuse and bind the soil particles. Acidic soils suffer most, because iron and calcium salts form hard complexes with soil particles under acid conditions. Other pans are man-made, compacted by repeated plowing, especially with moldboard plows, by heavy traffic or by pollution. Clay-rich soils compact easily, and sodium in wastewater can bind clay into a local pan, a common cause of septic system failure. Hardpans impede drainage and restrict roots on farms and in gardens. A broadfork, digging fork, spade or tractor-drawn chisel plow can break them. Manure, compost or peat improve drainage and encourage earthworms that slowly break pans. Lime and gypsum help with harder ones, though amendments may take years. {{ref:soil-water-242}} turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when wetted and dried again and again.

soil-form-033.title: Eluviation: how percolating water empties the upper soil
soil-form-033.text: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That removal of soil material from upper layers by percolating water is eluviation. It carries mineral and organic particles fine enough to stay suspended in water, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. That sets it apart from {{ref:soil-form-050}}, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. {{ref:soil-form-061}} is the extreme case, stripping out the oxides of iron and aluminum. The layer that loses material is an eluvial horizon. It may be a light-colored zone at the base of the surface mineral horizon, labelled Ae. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in {{ref:soil-form-009}}. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of {{ref:soil-form-032}}. On a slope the exchange also runs downhill: upper facets lose salts while lower facets gain them.

soil-form-057.title: Dynamic denudation: everything happening in the biomantle at once
soil-form-057.text: Plants' role in soil formation is well understood. The role of animals in making soil, horizons, the features in {{ref:soil-water-133}} and stone lines was poorly understood until recently. The dynamic form of {{ref:soil-water-272}} is the sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle. They include organic matter production, eluviation and illuviation, weathering, erosion and deposition, freeze–thaw, shrinking and swelling, and gravity movements. Normally all are subsidiary to animal mixing. Wilkinson and Humphreys offer evidence that this mixing appears to be the most active soil-forming process in many soils. It dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly the soils of {{ref:soil-class-106}} and {{ref:soil-class-024}}.

soil-form-084.title: Stone lines: geology or the work of burrowers?
soil-form-084.text: Few Earth-science topics have caused more controversy than the stone line. The argument spans archaeology, geology, the study of landforms, ecology and pedology, on every continent but Antarctica. At issue is whether stonelayers formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, ones. Sharpe coined 'stone-line' in 1938 from South Carolina, reading it as abiotic mass transfer on slopes. He was unaware of earlier names and drawings, including Darwin's. Others have read it as glacial evidence, or as an eroded pavement buried under tropical loess. Morrás and colleagues argued in 2009 that it is the base of soil biomantles. The literature remains divided, and an interpreter's view often reflects background and training.

soil-form-091.title: Glaciofluvial deposits, ice debris sorted by meltwater
soil-form-091.text: Meltwater sorts what the ice did not. Glaciofluvial deposits are boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited. They are laid down beside, below or downstream from the ice. As retreating glaciers carry this sediment downstream, they leave {{ref:soil-form-151}}. Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

soil-form-108.title: Non-glacial loess, dust from deserts and volcanoes
soil-form-108.text: Not all loess owes its origin to ice. Non-glacial loess comes from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or {{ref:soil-form-152}}, not from the sediment washed out of glaciers. Desert loess forms as wind-driven quartz grains abrade one another. Volcanic loess occurs in Ecuador and Argentina, and there are tropical and trade-wind kinds too. China's thick loess deposits blew in from deserts in the north of the country. Loess on the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Colorado is considered non-glacial desert loess, as is loess in Australia and Africa.

soil-found-018.title: What pushes a soil toward acid or alkaline
soil-found-018.text: Rain itself is slightly acidic. At an average pH of 5.6, from dissolved carbon dioxide, it washes basic cations out of soil and raises the share of aluminum and hydrogen ions. Many forces set a soil's pH, beginning with the minerals the soil formed from and the weathering they have undergone. In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products wash away. In dry climates, weaker weathering and less washing leave soils neutral or alkaline. Life adds acid too. Respiration and decay release CO2, and roots release H+ ions when plants take up more cations than anions, the negatively charged ions. Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidizing sulfide minerals in mine spoil or {{ref:soil-chem-030}} acidify further. Soils turn more alkaline with minerals rich in sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with bicarbonate-rich irrigation water. Where too little water flows through, carbonates and bicarbonates build up. Soils rich in calcium carbonate range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates.

soil-found-027.title: What red, gray and black soils reveal
soil-found-027.text: Soil colors are a code for what happens underground. Read correctly, they reveal how much soil organic matter a soil holds, along with its iron chemistry, aeration and salts. Dark brown or black usually means plenty of soil organic matter, which coats mineral grains and darkens them. Accumulated charcoal also turns soil black. Sodium helps {{ref:soil-bio-089}} disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark color extends. Red signals iron that has accumulated or oxidized in oxygen-rich, well-aerated soil. Yellow also reflects iron, but in less oxygen-rich settings. Gray or blue marks saturated soil without oxygen, where iron has been reduced or depleted. Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-196}}, melanterite and celadonite. White is common where salts, carbonates or calcite accumulate, often in arid environments, while {{ref:soil-chem-197}} can color acidic soils yellow. The {{ref:soil-form-010}} holds less of this dark material than the layer above. It takes its color, usually brownish or reddish, mainly from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}.

soil-found-035.title: Oxide minerals, where oxygen holds the metals
soil-found-035.text: The world's chief aluminum ore is a product of extreme weathering. This ore, {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, is a mixture of hydroxides that forms where chemical weathering is very intense. It belongs to the oxide minerals, those in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, or negatively charged ion. They fall into three groups: simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides. Corundum (Al2O3) and the iron oxide Fe2O3, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, belong to the corundum group of simple oxides. Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two charge states, Fe2+ and Fe3+, as {{ref:soil-chem-178}} explains. Oxides also form during weathering. Water converts many original rock minerals, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, to fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides through the reactions described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}.

soil-found-045.title: Soil organic matter, the once-living part of soil
soil-found-045.text: Most upland topsoils are only 1% to 6% organic material by mass, yet that thin share does an outsized amount of work. Soil organic matter is the organic part of soil. It takes in plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, the cells and tissues of soil microbes, and the substances those microbes make. It has three parts. The first is the living fraction covered in {{ref:soil-bio-269}}. The second is dead material, fresh and partly decomposed. The third is more stable organic carbon. Fresh litter lying on the surface is usually left out. Amounts vary enormously. Deserts hold under 1%, while low-lying wet soils can reach 90%. Soils with 12% to 18% organic carbon are generally classed as organic soils. It is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so a measurement of the organic carbon in a soil often stands in for it. Its benefits are many. It helps grains clump into crumbs, and improves water retention and biodiversity, holds back pollutants and buffers the soil against change. It also raises fertility. It offers sites that hold positively charged nutrients, and stores nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and micronutrients that microbes release slowly. How much builds up, and of what kind, depends on the kind of soil, which is set by the forces described in {{ref:soil-form-043}}. It is one ingredient of the mix described in {{ref:soil-found-078}}.

soil-found-058.title: Chemical weathering: rock remade for life at the surface
soil-found-058.text: Most rock is born hot and squeezed. It forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface. Chemical weathering is the result. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition. It does three things at once. It turns some of the minerals the rock formed with, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, into new secondary minerals. It carries other substances off in solution. And it leaves the most stable minerals unchanged, as a resistate. Water is the main agent. Through the reactions in {{ref:soil-found-060}}, it turns many of these original minerals into fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides. Oxygen oxidizes minerals, and carbon dioxide drives carbonation. The new set of minerals sits closer to equilibrium with surface conditions. True equilibrium is rare, though, because water keeps washing the dissolved products away. Chemical weathering is usually much more important than the mechanical kind in {{ref:soil-found-053}}. Mountains show its reach. Uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

soil-found-063.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock
soil-found-063.text: Two common minerals, albite and muscovite, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and {{ref:soil-bio-192}}. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as {{ref:soil-form-144}} or apatite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

soil-found-095.title: Pedology: reading how a soil came to be
soil-found-095.text: Every soil has a life story, and pedology sets out to read it. Pedology is the branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve, and builds frameworks for describing them, often where they lie in nature. Pedologists observe a soil's form, where soils occur and how they fit into wider settings of time and space. From those observations come classifications, soil maps and theories. As a soil forms, it slowly deepens and develops characteristic layers, approaching a steady state. Fallou conceived pedology in the 19th century as a fundamental science, separate from agrology, the applied forerunner of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. For a long time agronomists saw soil as a static production medium, while pedologists studied its ties to landscape history. The two approaches are now integrated. One sub-discipline characterizes and maps soils with numbers. Another, built on {{ref:soil-water-295}}, links landform processes with the way soils form.

soil-phys-036.title: The Unified Soil Classification System: soil in two letters
soil-phys-036.text: Engineers across North America describe a soil with just two letters. Those letters come from the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS, which classes soils by texture and grain size. It is the most common engineering classification in North America and works for most unconsolidated materials. The first letter names the main material: G for gravel, S for sand, M for silt, C for clay and O for organic soil. Peat gets PT. The second letter gives grading, W for well graded or P for poorly graded, or {{ref:soil-phys-022}}, H for high and L for low. Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained sands and gravels, fine-grained silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat. Sieves draw the first line. A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% stays on the No. 200 sieve, whose openings are 0.075 mm. The No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel. Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm. Sands and gravels are then divided by grain size and grading. Silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils. With 5–12% fines, the silt and clay particles, both grading and plasticity count. A dual symbol may then appear, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt. Europe's standard, {{ref:soil-class-152}}, is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-phys-063.title: Porosity: how much of a soil is empty space
soil-phys-063.text: Solid granite is almost all rock, with less than 0.005 of its volume left empty. Peat and clay can be more than half empty space. That share is porosity: the fraction of a material's total volume taken up by voids, given from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. Geologists, hydrologists and soil scientists use it for any of the materials described in {{ref:soil-phys-172}}, such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water. It is written ϕ or n. Porosity can be worked out from two densities. When the voids hold air, it equals one minus a ratio of two densities. On top is the density of the whole soil, in {{ref:soil-phys-060}}; below is that of its solid grains alone, in {{ref:soil-phys-062}}. Sorting matters as much as grain size. A well-sorted material is more porous than a poorly sorted one of similar size, because in the mixed one small particles fill the gaps between larger ones. A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity, and the ease of water flow, while making up only a small share of the volume. In rock and sedimentary layers, porosity governs how much water or hydrocarbon they may hold. It also falls with depth. As buried sediment compacts, its porosity drops exponentially, a pattern described by the Athy (1930) equation.

soil-phys-098.title: Pore water pressure, the push of water between grains
soil-phys-098.text: Water held between soil grains pushes back. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the groundwater in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock. Deep in saturated ground it is measured with piezometers. Where the water is not flowing it is close to hydrostatic, rising steadily with depth. The surface where it equals atmospheric pressure is the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Above that level, capillarity sets the pressure, and it is called tension, suction or matric pressure. Instruments with a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil measure it there, by methods set out in ISO 11276:1995. The pressure has several parts: the weight of overlying material, osmotic pressure from uneven ion concentrations, and pressure from water films, held by {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, that draw grains together. It matters because the load carried by the grains, {{ref:soil-phys-100}}, is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Too much of it can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer, as in {{ref:soil-phys-160}}.

soil-phys-118.title: Quicksand, solid until it is disturbed
soil-phys-118.text: At about 2 grams per cubic centimetre, quicksand is roughly twice as dense as the human body, so a person cannot sink beyond about waist height. It is a suspension of fine sand, silt or clay in water, a kind of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, that forms when saturated loose sand is agitated and loses its strength. Upward flow, as from an artesian spring, holds the grains suspended. Undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly makes it runny. Pulling a foot out at 1 cm/s takes as much force as lifting a car. Slow movements and floating on the back allow escape.

soil-phys-136.title: The penetrometer, a probe that tests the ground
soil-phys-136.text: The same kind of probe has tested farm fields, cricket pitches and the surface of Titan. A penetrometer tests the strength of a material such as soil by measuring how far a probe sinks into it. Soil penetrometers, usually round or cone-shaped, are dropped on or pressed into the ground. The depth of the hole shows, for example, whether it can carry a road. On farmland they measure how much compaction raises the resistance described in {{ref:soil-phys-176}}. Since 2009 they have also tested British racecourses.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice, the frost that grows in columns
soil-phys-159.text: On a cold night, bare soil can sprout a crop of ice. Needle ice is a mass of needle-shaped ice columns that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C. Water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. It depends on the process covered in {{ref:soil-phys-179}}: supercooled water, chilled below freezing yet still liquid, freezes onto existing ice in a porous material. Soils high in silt and in {{ref:soil-bio-114}} suit it best. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. The recorded maximum is 10 cm, though specimens of 15–20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg. Needle ice is frost heaving at its earliest, with no overlying soil to lift. The needles raise soil particles and crusts that settle unevenly when they melt. This disturbs streambanks, aids soil creep and helps shape {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Heaved seedlings often die, because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. The ice has many names: frost pillars, Kammeis, shimobashira, and pipkrake, a Swedish term coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman.

soil-phys-192.title: How pollution travels with moving groundwater
soil-phys-192.text: A spill on the surface can turn up years later in a distant well. Contaminant transport in groundwater is the movement of dissolved contaminants with the water flowing underground, and contaminant hydrogeology is the field that studies it, a branch of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Some contaminants are man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides. Others are natural, such as arsenic or salinity. Three main mechanisms move them. {{ref:soil-phys-193}} carries them at seepage velocity. Diffusion spreads them from high to low concentration. Dispersion, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-194}}, spreads them further still. Diffusion and dispersion only spread a contaminant, though. Sticking to the soil, the process of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, does something different: it slows the contaminant's average velocity. Precipitation and decay also change what arrives. So the properties of the {{ref:soil-phys-201}}, beyond the flow itself, shape where pollution goes. Polluted groundwater forms a plume, and its advancing edge can reach wells and springs. Hydrologists track it with transport and groundwater models.

soil-phys-205.title: Interflow: water that slips sideways through the soil
soil-phys-205.text: Not all water that soaks in heads straight down. Interflow is the lateral movement of water through the unsaturated zone that returns to the surface or enters a stream. It happens when infiltrated water meets hydraulic conductivity that decreases with depth and turns downslope. Throughflow is the part of interflow that returns to the surface as overland flow before reaching a stream or groundwater. If the subsurface saturates, interflow may exfiltrate as return flow and join the overland flow. Interflow and the underground tunneling of {{ref:soil-water-289}} can erode gullies, just as surface runoff does.

soil-phys-218.title: Crop coefficients: from reference grass to real crop
soil-phys-218.text: Watering plans, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-234}}, turn a weather figure into a crop's thirst with one multiplier. The crop coefficient, Kc, is most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop. Multiplying ET0 by Kc gives the crop's actual water requirement, ETc. Kc changes through the season with growth stage, often following a trapezoidal or leaf area index curve. It can exceed 1 when the crop uses more water than the reference. Stress coefficients between 0 and 1, most often for water stress (Kw), are multiplied in to reduce the estimate.

soil-water-026.title: The tipping point where a rill is born
soil-water-026.text: A rill starts at a tipping point. Rill initiation is the moment when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and water begins to tear particles loose. Sandy and loamy soils are especially prone to rills, while dense clays resist them. Slope steepness mainly controls whether rills form and how deep they cut. Slope length and soil permeability set how many form. Each soil has a threshold slope below which rills cannot form. On many non-cohesive slopes it is about 2 degrees, at a drag speed of 3 to 3.5 cm/s, the measure explained in {{ref:soil-water-282}}. Once rills exist, their walls add to the loss. Up to 37% of erosion in rilled areas may come from collapsing sidewalls undercut and weakened by water.

soil-water-043.title: Predicting erosion, and why the forecasts often miss
soil-water-043.text: Predicted and observed erosion rates often differ widely. Erosion prediction uses data and models to forecast where, and how fast, erosion may happen. There are dozens of models. Some treat long-term natural erosion as part of landscape evolution, while many quantify erosion sped up by people. Most predict average annual soil loss from a plot, field or catchment under different land management. Most consider only water erosion. Few predict wind erosion, and models of {{ref:soil-water-038}} or gully erosion are rare. Process-based models solve equations for detachment, transport and deposition. Empirical models relate soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors. No model is fully process-based yet. Research favors process-based models, but the empirical USLE remains the standard for conservation planning. Two widely used North American models are the revised version of the USLE, {{ref:soil-water-291}}, and the Water Erosion Prediction Project model, {{ref:soil-water-111}}. Unless calibrated locally, models remain better research tools than regulatory instruments. They are also non-linear, which makes it hard or impossible to scale predictions from small plots up to large areas.

soil-water-109.title: Grassed waterways, green lines down the valley floor
soil-water-109.text: Storm runoff from cropland gathers along the lowest line of a valley. There it can cut rills and gullies that speed the water on and worsen the damage downstream. A grassed waterway guards that line against erosion. It is a strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the floor of a cultivated dry valley. The grass raises soil cohesion and roughness, prevents rills and gullies, slows runoff and lets it soak back in during long winter rains. It cannot reabsorb runoff from heavy spring and summer storms, so earthen dams across it may be added to hold the flow back for a while. The grass strips of {{ref:soil-water-290}} are different. They are narrower, only a few meters wide, and placed along rivers or along or within fields.

soil-water-168.title: Measuring soil moisture without digging it up
soil-water-168.text: Soil moisture can now be gauged by a probe in one field or by satellite imagery combined with hydrological models. Soil moisture measurement means estimating water content in place, instead of drying samples. Several geophysical methods do it, among them {{ref:soil-water-223}}, {{ref:soil-water-170}}, {{ref:soil-water-226}} and {{ref:soil-water-225}}. Others include amplitude domain reflectometry, {{ref:soil-meth-015}} and {{ref:soil-meth-014}}. Geophysical sensors often monitor soil moisture continuously for agriculture and research. Each method has strengths and weaknesses, so combining techniques can reduce the drawbacks of any one. Some farmers now schedule irrigation from these readings, a practice called smart irrigation.

soil-water-212.title: Refilling aquifers on purpose
soil-water-212.text: In Orange County, California, one facility cleans and injects 100 million gallons of water a day, or 90 billion gallons a year. That is artificial groundwater recharge: recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface. Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells. In India, farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater. In 2007 the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states. Cities face a related task. Stormwater pollution collects in {{ref:soil-water-090}}, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and the planted basins of {{ref:soil-env-308}} should be designed.

soil-water-255.title: Four letters that rank soils by runoff
soil-water-255.text: The NRCS sorts soils into four hydrologic soil groups, A to D, by how readily they take in water. The group is used to choose a {{ref:soil-water-088}}. Group A, mostly deep, well-drained sands and gravels, has a final infiltration rate above 7.6 mm (0.30 in) per hour and low runoff potential. Group B takes in 3.8 to 7.6 mm per hour. Group C, often with an impeding layer or fine texture, manages 1.3 to 3.8 mm. Group D has high runoff potential. It covers swelling clays, soils with a permanent high water table or a claypan near the surface, and shallow soils over impervious material. The group is picked from measured infiltration rates, a survey such as the NRCS online one described in {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, or a soil professional's judgment.
